szoveg_eredeti:
The higher the climb, the greater the fall. The Nasdaq, the American stock market index specializing in technology stocks, proved this on Thursday, November 5. With a 5.5% plunge, it logged its worst session since April 2025 and its biggest one-day points loss on record. More than $2.5 trillion in market capitalization was wiped out in 24 hours.

After reaching record highs in October, fueled by stratospheric valuations, concerns over the bursting of a speculative bubble around artificial intelligence have resurfaced. Even though Friday's session ended with a slight rebound, this sudden drop serves as a reminder of the fragility of the sector's growth and profitability expectations.

The Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, likely acted as a catalyst, as many observers had expected a market correction. The election results made the risk of tighter regulation over AI development more real. In several states, local initiatives aiming to restrict the establishment of data centers resonated with voters. The significant electricity and water consumption of these facilities, their impact on local areas, and the costs they impose on local populations have met with growing opposition.

Wall Street must recognize that this technological revolution cannot unfold independently from physical constraints and the consent of citizens. From this standpoint, Thursday's market drop serve as a timely reality check.

The spectacular enthusiasm for AI drove company valuations in the sector to levels based more on bets than on a rational assessment of their growth potential. In recent months, demand for computing power to run AI models seemed inexhaustible. Funding, often secured through borrowing, poured in on the assumption that revenues would eventually follow. Yet, obstacles related to building the infrastructure essential for AI's development have been mounting, while questions about investment profitability have multiplied.

The danger now extends beyond just financial markets. In a matter of months, AI has become one of the main engines of the United States' economic growth. The hundreds of billions of dollars invested in data centers have supported economic activity, while soaring stock prices have fueled a wealth effect favorable to consumer spending. A lasting loss of confidence could trigger a vicious cycle, with less funding, delayed projects, and declining activity. After having been one of the main drivers of the American economy, AI could become its Achilles' heel.

However, it is premature to interpret this setback as a rejection of the technology itself. Financial markets anticipated the benefits of this revolution without sufficiently considering the costs it imposes on society. Beyond the excesses of speculation, this correction reminds us that the development of AI depends not only on the billions of dollars investors are willing to pour in, but also on what people are prepared to accept. That the markets are beginning to grasp this would be progress.
